questions.question: As per Article 170 of the Constitution of India, the Legislative Assembly of each State shall consist of NOT more than __________ members.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**500**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Article 170 of the Constitution of India deals with the composition of the Legislative Assemblies of States.
 
• The Legislative Assembly of each State shall consist of not more than 500 and not less than 60 members.
 
• This limitation ensures that the size of the Legislative Assembly is manageable and can effectively represent the population of the state.
 
• There are exceptions to this rule, such as in the cases of smaller states like Sikkim, which have fewer than 60 members due to their smaller population.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Legislative Assembly:

 
 
• Also known as Vidhan Sabha, it is the lower house of the state legislature in India.
 
• Members of the Legislative Assembly (MLAs) are directly elected by the people of the state.
 
• The term of the Legislative Assembly is five years, unless dissolved sooner.
 
• The Assembly is responsible for making laws on subjects enumerated in the State List of the Constitution.
 
 
 
• Article 170:
 
 
• This article of the Indian Constitution specifies the composition of the Legislative Assemblies of States.
 
• It sets the maximum and minimum limits for the number of members in a state's Legislative Assembly.
 
• The size of each Legislative Assembly is based on the population of the state as per the last Census.
 
 
 
• Exceptions:
 
 
• Some states with smaller populations, such as Sikkim, Goa, and Mizoram, have Legislative Assemblies with fewer than 60 members.
 
• These exceptions are made to accommodate the unique demographic and geographic characteristics of these states.
 
 
 
• State List:
 
 
• The State List is a list of subjects under the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India.
 
• It enumerates the areas in which only the state governments can legislate.
 
• Examples of subjects in the State List include police, public health, and agriculture.

questions.question: According to the National Jute Board 2022-23, which state is the largest producer of jute?

• West Bengal alone accounts for over 50 percent raw jute production.
 
• The leading world's jute producing countries are India , Bangladesh , China and Thailand .

• Jute crop requires humid climate with temperature fluctuating between 24 degree Celsius and 38 degree Celsius.
 
• Minimum rainfall required for jute cultivation is 1000 mm .
 
• New grey alluvial soil of good depth receiving silt from annual floods is most suitable for jute growth.
 
• However, jute is grown widely in sandy looms and clay loams.

questions.question: The density of population in India (Census 2011) is __________________ persons per sq km.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**382**__.

__
 
• The density of population in India is calculated by dividing the total population of India by the total area of the country.
 
• As per the 2011 Census, the total population of India was 1.21 billion and the total area was 3.17 million sq km.
 
• Therefore, the density of population in India in 2011 was 382 persons/sq km.
 
• This density is relatively high, considering the fact that India is the second-most populous country in the world after China.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The definition of a census is the process of gathering and recording data regarding the population. 
 
• The first comprehensive census was done in 1881, but it had been conducted every ten years since Viceroy Lord Mayo took office in 1872.
 
• Since 1949, it has been managed by the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India, through the Registrar General and Census Commissioner of India.

questions.question: Which of the following rivers passes through the maximum number of states in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ganga**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• River Ganga:

 
 
• The River Ganga originates from the Gangotri glacier in Uttarakhand.
 
• Alaknanda River joins Bhagirathi at Devprayag and from there the river is called Ganga.
 
• Yamuna(Largest right bank tributary of Ganga), Damodar (Sorrow of Bengal), Ghagra, Gomti, Gandak, Ramganga, Kosi (Sorrow of Bihar), Son, Mahananda are major tributaries of River Ganga.
 
• It flows through the states of Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Jharkhand, and West Bengal.
 
• It is a transboundary river, flows through India and Bangladesh.
 
• The total length of the river is 2525 km
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Damodar River**

 
 
• The origin of Damodar River is the Chotanagpur plateau (Culha Pani of Lohardaga district) and the estuary is Hooghly.
 
• It is the longest, largest and most polluted river of Jharkhand.
 
• The main tributaries of Damodar River are Barakar, Konar, Jamunia, Bokaro and Katari.
 
• Damodar River is also known as Dev River.
 
• Its drainage area is Hazaribagh, Chatra, Dhanbad, Bokaro, Ranchi, Latehar and Lohardaga.
 
• Damodar River is the most important river of Jharkhand which flows through a rift or fault valley.
 
• Damodar River is also known as Damuda. Damu means holy and da means water. 
 
• The Damodar River is a rain-fed river with a prolonged dry season followed by a turbulent monsoon.
 
• The river's basin area is 23,371 km² and is known for its mineral resources and large-scale mining and industrial activity.
 
• Damodar River was earlier a very dangerous river due to the severity of floods, due to which it was also known as the Sorrow of Bengal.
 
 
 
• **Indus River**
 
 
• The Indus River is one of the longest rivers in the world, with a length of approximately 2900 kilometers.
 
• It originates in the Tibetan Plateau near Lake Mansarovar in China.
 
• The Indus River flows through the regions of Ladakh in India and the entire length of Pakistan before emptying into the Arabian Sea near Karachi.
 
• The river plays a crucial role in the irrigation and agriculture of the region, particularly in Pakistan, where it is the primary water source for the country's breadbasket.
 
 
 
• **Mahanadi River**
 
• The Mahanadi river has its source in the Dhamtari district of Chhattisgarh, about 6 kilometers from the village of Pharsiya. 
 
• The river then flows through Chhattisgarh and Odisha before emptying into the Bay of Bengal. 
 
• The Mahanadi is the third largest river in peninsular India after the Godavari and Krishna rivers. 
 
• It is a major source of water for irrigation, drinking, and hydroelectric power generation in the two states.
 
• Here are some other interesting facts about the Mahanadi river:
 
 
• ​The name "Mahanadi" comes from the Sanskrit words "maha" (great) and "nadi" (river).
 
• The Mahanadi is about 900 kilometers long.
 
• The river's drainage basin covers an area of about 132,000 square kilometers.
 
• The Mahanadi has a number of tributaries, including the Seonath, Hasdeo, Mand, and Ib rivers.
 
• The Hirakud Dam, the longest earthen dam in the world, is located on the Mahanadi river.
 
• 
 
The Mahanadi is an important economic resource for the states of Chhattisgarh and Odisha.

questions.question: The correct order of percentage of gases in atmosphere is:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**N2>O2>Ar>CO2**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

**Earth's Atmosphere:**

__
 
• **Composition:** Primarily nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%), with trace amounts of argon, carbon dioxide, and other gases.
 
• **Layers:** Troposphere (where weather occurs), stratosphere (contains the ozone layer), mesosphere (where meteors burn up), thermosphere (where auroras occur), and exosphere (the outermost layer).
 
• **Importance:** Essential for life, providing breathable air, regulating temperature, protecting from harmful radiation, and driving weather patterns.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lithosphere**

 
 
• The Lithosphere is the rigid, outermost shell of the Earth, encompassing both the crust and the uppermost part of the mantle.
 
• It is divided into tectonic plates that float on the semi-fluid asthenosphere beneath it.
 
• The thickness of the Lithosphere varies, being thinnest at mid-ocean ridges and thickest beneath continental crust.
 
• The Lithosphere is crucial for plate tectonics, as its movements and interactions cause earthquakes, volcanic activity, and the creation of mountain ranges.
 
 

 
• Stratosphere

 
 
• The Stratosphere is the second major layer of Earth's atmosphere, lying above the Troposphere and below the Mesosphere.
 
• It extends from about 10 km to 50 km above Earth's surface.
 
• This layer contains the ozone layer, which absorbs and scatters ultraviolet solar radiation.
 
• Commercial jet aircraft typically fly in the lower stratosphere.
 
 
 
• Troposphere
 
 
• The Troposphere is the lowest layer of Earth's atmosphere, extending from Earth's surface up to about 8-15 km.
 
• It contains approximately 75% of the atmosphere's mass and 99% of its water vapor and aerosols.
 
• Weather events occur in the Troposphere.
 
 
 
• Mesosphere
 
 
• The Mesosphere is the layer of the atmosphere above the Stratosphere and below the Thermosphere.
 
• It extends from about 50 km to 85 km above the Earth's surface.
 
• This layer is where most meteorites burn up upon entering the Earth's atmosphere.
 
• The temperature decreases with altitude in the Mesosphere.

__
 
• ** Sarhul:**

 
 
• **Tribal Celebration:** Sarhul is a significant festival celebrated by the Munda, Ho, Oraon, and Santhal tribes of Jharkhand, Odisha, and West Bengal in India. It marks the beginning of the new year in the tribal Sarna religion.
 
• **Nature Worship:** Sarhul is deeply connected to nature. The festival celebrates the sal tree (Shorea robusta) and its blossoming, which is a sign of the arrival of spring. The sal tree holds immense cultural and religious significance for these tribes.
 
• **Spring Festival:** It is a spring festival, usually celebrated in the Hindu month of Chaitra, which corresponds to March-April. The exact date varies depending on the lunar calendar.
 
• **Rituals and Offerings:** The festival involves various rituals, including the offering of prayers to the village deity (Gram Devta) and the sal trees. The priests, known as 'Pahan' or 'Pujari', play a crucial role in the ceremonies. Offerings of rice beer (Handia), new fruits, and flowers are made.
 
• **Dance and Music:** Sarhul is a joyous occasion marked by traditional dances and music. The 'Sarhul dance' is a special highlight, performed by both men and women in colorful attire. Drums, flutes, and other traditional instruments accompany the dances.
 
• **Community Bonding:** The festival is a time for community bonding and social gatherings. People come together to celebrate, share food and drinks, and participate in the festivities. It strengthens social ties and reinforces cultural identity.
 
• **Significance of Sal Blossoms:** The sal blossoms are a central symbol of Sarhul. They represent new life, renewal, and the fertility of nature. The tribals use sal leaves and flowers in their rituals and decorations.
 
• **Agricultural Significance:** Sarhul also has agricultural significance, as it marks the beginning of the agricultural cycle. The tribals believe that the blessings of the deities will ensure a good harvest.
 
• **Preservation of Culture:** Sarhul plays a vital role in preserving the tribal culture and traditions. It is a way for the tribals to connect with their roots and pass on their heritage to future generations.
 
• **Tourism Potential:** Sarhul is a unique and colorful festival that has the potential to attract tourists and promote cultural tourism in the region.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Chhath Puja:**

 
 
• **Sun Worship:** Chhath Puja is a major Hindu festival dedicated to Surya, the Sun God. It is primarily observed in the states of Bihar, Jharkhand, Uttar Pradesh, and parts of Nepal.
 
• **Vedic Origins:** The festival has ancient Vedic origins and is mentioned in various scriptures. It is believed that performing Chhath Puja bestows blessings of health, wealth, and prosperity.
 
• **Four-Day Festival:** Chhath Puja is a four-day festival, with each day having its own significance and rituals. The rituals include fasting, bathing in holy waters, and offering prayers to the Sun God.
 
• **Strict Observances:** The festival involves strict observances, including a 36-hour fast without water and food. Devotees observe celibacy and maintain purity during the festival.
 
• **Offerings to the Sun:** The main ritual of Chhath Puja involves offering 'Arghya' (obeisance) to the setting and rising sun. Devotees stand in waist-deep water and offer prayers, along with fruits, flowers, and other offerings, to the Sun God.
 
• **Significance of 'Supa' and 'Daliya':** 'Supa' (winnowing fan) and 'Daliya' (basket) are important ritualistic items used during Chhath Puja. They are filled with offerings and carried by devotees to the river banks.
 
• **Community Participation:** Chhath Puja is a community festival, with families and neighbors coming together to celebrate. The atmosphere is filled with devotion, music, and folk songs.
 
• **Cleanliness and Purity:** Cleanliness and purity are paramount during Chhath Puja. The surroundings are kept clean, and devotees maintain a high level of personal hygiene.
 
• **Fasting and Devotion:** The rigorous fasting and devotion displayed by devotees during Chhath Puja are remarkable. It is a testament to their faith and belief in the power of the Sun God.
 
• **Environmental Consciousness:** Chhath Puja also promotes environmental consciousness, as it involves worshipping the Sun, water, and nature. It highlights the importance of respecting and preserving the environment.
 
 
 
• **Maghi (Makar Sankranti):**
 
 
• **Solar Festival:** Maghi, also known as Makar Sankranti, is a Hindu festival dedicated to Surya, the Sun God. It marks the sun's transit into the Makara (Capricorn) zodiac sign.
 
• **Winter Solstice:** It usually falls on January 14th or 15th every year and marks the end of the winter solstice and the beginning of longer days. It's a significant harvest festival.
 
• **Auspicious Time:** Makar Sankranti is considered an auspicious time for undertaking new ventures and charitable activities. It is believed that donating to the needy during this time brings good fortune.
 
• **Ritual Bath:** Taking a holy dip in rivers or other water bodies is a common ritual on Makar Sankranti. It is believed to cleanse the body and soul. Special gatherings are held at holy places.
 
• **Tilgul and Sweets:** The exchange of 'Tilgul' (sesame seeds and jaggery sweets) is a characteristic feature of Makar Sankranti, particularly in Maharashtra. It symbolizes friendship and goodwill.
 
• **Kite Flying:** Kite flying is a popular tradition associated with Makar Sankranti in many parts of India. The skies are filled with colorful kites, creating a festive atmosphere.
 
• **Harvest Festival:** Makar Sankranti is also a harvest festival, celebrating the reaping of crops and the arrival of spring. It is a time to express gratitude for the bounty of nature.
 
• **Regional Variations:** The festival is celebrated in different ways in different parts of India. While the core theme of worshipping the Sun remains the same, the rituals and traditions vary.
 
• **Pongal in South India:** In South India, Makar Sankranti is celebrated as Pongal, a major harvest festival. It is a four-day festival, with each day having its own significance.
 
• **Lohri in North India:** In North India, Makar Sankranti is preceded by Lohri, a bonfire festival. People gather around bonfires, sing folk songs, and offer prayers to the fire god.
 
 
 
• **Dang Darbar:**

• **Religious Significance:** The festival has religious significance and is associated with the worship of various deities. It is a time for prayers, rituals, and offerings.

• **Folk Music and Dance:** Folk music and dance are an integral part of the Dang Darbar. The tribals perform traditional dances and sing folk songs, accompanied by traditional musical instruments.
 
• **Colorful Attire:** The tribals wear colorful attire during the festival, adding to the vibrant atmosphere. They adorn themselves with traditional jewelry and accessories.
 
• **Cultural Performances:** The Dang Darbar features various cultural performances, including plays, skits, and storytelling sessions. These performances showcase the rich cultural heritage of the Dangi people.
 
• **Local Crafts and Cuisine:** The festival also provides a platform for local artisans and craftspeople to showcase their products. Visitors can sample traditional Dangi cuisine and purchase local handicrafts.
 
• **Tourism Attraction:** The Dang Darbar is a unique cultural event that attracts tourists from across India and beyond. It offers a glimpse into the tribal way of life and the rich cultural traditions of the Dang region.
 
• **Preservation of Tribal Culture:** The festival plays a vital role in preserving the tribal culture and traditions of the Dangi people. It is a way for them to connect with their roots and pass on their heritage to future generations.
 
• **Community Bonding:** The Dang Darbar is a time for community bonding and social harmony. It strengthens social ties and reinforces the sense of belonging among the Dangi peoples.

questions.question: Which of the following books was written by Kautilya, Prime Minister of Chandragupta Maurya?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Arthashstra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__

• After Alexander the Great's incursion into India in 326 BC, there was a period of political vacuum and disarray in the northwest regions of the subcontinent.

questions.question: The garbhagriha and shikhara are made in a Rekha-Prasada or Latina style and the mandapa of an old form of wooden architecture. These features of temple architecture are present in which part of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Northern**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

**Garbhagriha:**

 
• **The Sanctum Sanctorum:** The *garbhagriha* is the most sacred chamber within a Hindu temple. It houses the primary deity (the *murt*i or idol) and is considered the dwelling place of the divine within the temple complex. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
• **Small and Square:** Typically, the *garbhagriha* is a small, windowless, and square-shaped room. Its simplicity emphasizes its sacred nature, focusing attention on the deity within. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
• **Symbolic Significance:** The *garbhagriha* represents the womb of the universe, symbolizing the origin of creation and the source of divine energy. It's a space of profound spiritual significance for devotees.
 
• **Placement:** The *garbhagriha* is usually located at the very heart of the temple, directly beneath the towering *shikhara* (spire). This placement reinforces the connection between the deity and the cosmic axis.
 
• **Access:** Access to the *garbhagriha* is often restricted, with only priests or authorized individuals allowed to enter. This preserves the sanctity of the inner sanctum. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
• **Pradakshina Patha:** Often, a narrow circumambulatory path, the *pradakshina patha*, surrounds the *garbhagriha*, allowing devotees to walk around the sanctum in a clockwise direction as a mark of reverence. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

**Shikhara (Rekha-Prasada/Latina Style):**

 
• **The Towering Spire:** The *shikhara* is the prominent superstructure that rises above the *garbhagriha* in North Indian temples (Nagara style). It's a visual marker of the temple's presence and a symbolic representation of the cosmic mountain, Meru. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
• **Rekha-Prasada/Latina:** This specific type of *shikhara* is characterized by its tall, slender, and curvilinear shape. It resembles a gradually inclining line (hence "rekha") and is often referred to as "Latina" due to its similarity to the shape of a Latin sail.

questions.question: Bacteria are the sole members of which of the following kingdoms?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Monera**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Monera (or Bacteria and Archaea)**

 
 
• Prokaryotic Cells: Monerans are characterized by their simple cell structure. They lack a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles. Their genetic material (DNA) is not enclosed within a membrane.
 
• Unicellular: Monerans are single-celled organisms, although they may live in colonies.
 
• Diverse Metabolism: They exhibit a wide range of metabolic strategies. Some are autotrophs (making their own food like plants), while others are heterotrophs (relying on external food sources like animals).
 
• Reproduction: Monerans typically reproduce asexually through binary fission, where one cell divides into two identical cells.
 
• Ubiquitous: They are found in virtually all habitats on Earth, from extreme environments like hot springs and deep sea vents to more familiar places like soil and the human body.
 
• Ecological Roles: Monerans play crucial roles in nutrient cycling, decomposition, and various symbiotic relationships.
 
• Examples: Bacteria like E. coli and Streptococcus, as well as archaea like methanogens and halophiles.
 
• Cell Wall: Most monerans have a cell wall, but its composition differs from that of plants and fungi.
 
• Motility: Some monerans are motile, using flagella or other mechanisms to move.
 
• Genetic Diversity: Despite their simple structure, monerans have a high degree of genetic diversity, allowing them to adapt to a wide range of conditions.
 
• Human Impact: Monerans have a profound impact on human life, both beneficial (e.g., in food production and our gut microbiome) and harmful (e.g., causing diseases).
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Animalia (Animals)**

 
 
• Eukaryotic Cells: Animals have complex cells with a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
 
• Multicellular: Animals are multicellular organisms with specialized cells organized into tissues and organs.
 
• Heterotrophic Nutrition: Animals are heterotrophs, meaning they cannot make their own food and must consume other organisms for energy.
 
• Mobility: Most animals are motile at some stage in their life cycle, allowing them to actively seek food and mates.
 
• Sexual Reproduction: Animals typically reproduce sexually, with the fusion of sperm and egg cells.
 
• No Cell Walls: Animal cells lack cell walls, which allows for greater flexibility and movement.
 
• Diverse Forms: The animal kingdom is incredibly diverse, encompassing a vast range of organisms from sponges to insects to mammals.
 
• Ecological Roles: Animals play diverse ecological roles, including predators, prey, herbivores, decomposers, and pollinators.
 
• Examples: Insects, fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals, including humans.
 
• Nervous System: Most animals have a nervous system that allows them to sense and respond to their environment.
 
• Digestive System: Animals have a digestive system to break down food and absorb nutrients.
 
 
 
• **Plantae (Plants)**
 
 
• Eukaryotic Cells: Plant cells have a nucleus, membrane-bound organelles, and a rigid cell wall made of cellulose.
 
• Multicellular: Plants are multicellular organisms with specialized tissues and organs, such as roots, stems, and leaves.
 
• Autotrophic Nutrition: Plants are primarily autotrophs, using photosynthesis to convert sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide into sugars for energy.
 
• Immobile (Mostly): Most plants are rooted in place and cannot move freely like animals.
 
• Sexual and Asexual Reproduction: Plants can reproduce both sexually and asexually, depending on the species.
 
• Chlorophyll: Plants contain chlorophyll, a green pigment that absorbs sunlight for photosynthesis.
 
• Ecological Importance: Plants are essential for life on Earth, producing oxygen, forming the base of most food chains, and providing habitats.
 
• Examples: Mosses, ferns, conifers, and flowering plants.
 
• Adaptations: Plants have evolved a wide array of adaptations to survive in different environments.
 
• Alternation of Generations: Plants exhibit a life cycle called alternation of generations, alternating between haploid and diploid stages.
 
• Economic Importance: Plants provide humans with food, medicine, timber, and other resources.
 
 
 
• **Protista (Protists)**
 
 
• Eukaryotic Cells: Protists have eukaryotic cells with a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
 
• Unicellular or Multicellular: Protists can be unicellular (like amoebas) or multicellular (like some algae).
 
• Diverse Nutrition: Protists exhibit a wide range of nutritional strategies, including autotrophy, heterotrophy, and mixotrophy (combining both).
 
• Diverse Structures: Protists are a very diverse group, and their body structures vary greatly.
 
• Reproduction: Protists can reproduce both sexually and asexually, depending on the species.
 
• Habitats: They are found in a variety of moist environments, including water, soil, and even inside other organisms.
 
• Ecological Roles: Protists play important roles in aquatic food webs, as well as in various symbiotic relationships.
 
• Examples: Algae (like seaweed), protozoa (like amoebas and paramecium), and slime molds.
 
• Evolutionary Significance: Protists are a diverse group that includes some of the earliest eukaryotes, providing insights into the evolution of more complex organisms.
 
• Parastic Protists: Some protists are parasites that can cause diseases in humans and other animals (e.g., malaria).
 
• Classification Challenges: Because of their diversity, classifying protists has been a long-standing challenge for biologists.

• While the statement that Hampi was "discovered" in 1800 is a simplification, it's true that the ruins of this magnificent city were brought to wider attention around that time. Here's a more nuanced explanation:
 
• Hampi's History Before 1800

• Local Communities: Hampi is also home to local communities who have lived in the area for generations. Their lives and traditions are intertwined with the history of the site.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true with regard to the establishment of Central Public Sector Undertakings in India?

questions.question: Contingency Fund of India is operated by the __________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Executive action**__.

__
 
• The Contingency Fund of India is established under Article 267 of the Constitution of India.
 
• This fund is used to meet unforeseen expenditures that cannot wait for the authorization of the Parliament.
 
• The Contingency Fund of India is at the disposal of the President of India.
 
• It is operated by the executive branch of the Government, specifically the Ministry of Finance.
 
• The fund is placed at the disposal of the President to enable advances to be made for meeting unforeseen expenditure, pending authorization by the Parliament.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Parliamentary Approval:**

 
 
• Any expenditure from the Contingency Fund needs subsequent approval from the Parliament.
 
• The amount withdrawn is recouped to the fund after Parliament authorizes the necessary expenditure through the Appropriation Acts.
 
 
 
• **Amount in the Fund:**
 
 
• The corpus of the Contingency Fund of India is Rs. 500 crore.
 
• This amount can be modified by the Parliament if needed.
 
 
 
• **State Contingency Funds:**
 
 
• States in India also have their own contingency funds for meeting urgent and unforeseen expenditures.
 
• The operation of state contingency funds is similar to that of the central fund, controlled by the respective state governments.
 
 
 
• **Similar Funds:**
 
 
• Other specific funds like the Consolidated Fund of India and Public Account of India also play crucial roles in the financial management of the country.
 
• The Consolidated Fund is the chief fund where all revenues received by the government, loans raised, and money received in repayment of loans are credited.

questions.question: The process of depositing a layer of any desired metal on another material by means of electricity is called ____________.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**electroplating**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Electroplating is a process used to coat the surface of a metal with a thin layer of another metal using an electric current.
 
• It is commonly used for decorative purposes, corrosion protection, and to improve wear resistance.
 
• The process involves immersing both the item to be plated and the plating metal in an electrolyte solution and applying a current.
 
• The plating metal acts as the anode, and the item to be plated acts as the cathode, causing metal ions to move and deposit on the item.
 
• Materials commonly used for electroplating include gold, silver, nickel, and chromium.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Electrolysis:**

 
 
• Electrolysis is a broader term that refers to the decomposition of a substance by passing an electric current through it.
 
• It is used in various applications, including electroplating, electrorefining, and electrolysis of water to produce hydrogen and oxygen.
 
 
 
• **Anode and Cathode:**
 
 
• In electroplating, the anode is the metal that will be deposited, and the cathode is the item that is being plated.
 
• The anode is positively charged, while the cathode is negatively charged.
 
 
 
• **Electrolyte Solution:**
 
 
• The electrolyte solution is a liquid that contains ions and conducts electricity, facilitating the movement of metal ions from the anode to the cathode.
 
• Common electrolytes include solutions of metal salts, such as copper sulfate for copper plating.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Electroplating:**
 
 
• Electroplating is used in various industries, including automotive, jewelry, electronics, and aerospace.
 
• It enhances the appearance, durability, and conductivity of the plated items.

questions.question: Which is the following is abolished, and its practice forbidden in any form, according to Article 17 of the Constitution?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Untouchability**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 17 of the Indian Constitution explicitly abolishes **untouchability** and forbids its practice in any form.
 
• The abolition of untouchability is a fundamental right under Part III of the Constitution.
 
• The enforcement of any disability arising out of untouchability is an offense punishable by law.
 
• This Article aims to eradicate social discrimination and promote equality among all citizens of India.
 
• It is supported by the **Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955**, which prescribes punishments for practices of untouchability.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955**

 
 
• This Act was enacted to enforce the provisions of Article 17 of the Constitution.
 
• It prescribes penalties for preventing anyone from entering public places or using public facilities due to untouchability.
 
• Violators can face imprisonment and fines, ensuring the eradication of untouchability practices.
 
 
 
• **Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989**
 
 
• This Act provides specific measures to prevent atrocities against Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.
 
• It also addresses issues of discrimination and social injustice faced by these communities.
 
• The Act includes provisions for special courts to expedite the trial of offenses under it.
 
 
 
• **Fundamental Rights**
 
 
• Part III of the Indian Constitution enshrines the fundamental rights guaranteed to all citizens.
 
• These rights include equality before the law, freedom of speech, and protection against discrimination.
 
• Article 17 is part of this section, emphasizing the right to equality.
 
 
 
• **Social Equality**
 
 
• Social equality refers to a state where all individuals within a society have equal rights and opportunities.
 
• Efforts to promote social equality in India include various legal measures and affirmative action policies.
 
• These measures aim to uplift marginalized communities and ensure their inclusion in mainstream society.

questions.question: Lost wax casting technique was used to make _________ statues during Harappan civilisation.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**bronze**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The lost wax casting technique was primarily used to create **bronze statues** during the Harappan civilization.
 
• This technique involved creating a wax model of the statue, which was then covered in clay to form a mold.
 
• The wax was melted and drained away, leaving a hollow mold, into which molten bronze was poured.
 
• After the bronze cooled and solidified, the clay mold was broken away to reveal the finished statue.
 
• The famous "Dancing Girl" statue found in Mohenjo-Daro is one of the most well-known examples of this technique.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Lost Wax Casting Technique**:

 
 
• This ancient method is also known as "cire perdue" and has been used for thousands of years.
 
• It allows for intricate and detailed designs that are difficult to achieve with other casting methods.
 
• The technique was not only used in the Harappan civilization but also in various other ancient cultures around the world.
 
 
 
• **The Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-Daro**:
 
 
• This statue is about 10.8 cm high and depicts a young woman in a dancing pose.
 
• It is one of the earliest known bronze sculptures in the world, dating back to around 2500 BCE.
 
 
 
• **Harappan Civilization**:
 
 
• The Harappan civilization, also known as the Indus Valley Civilization, flourished around 2600-1900 BCE.
 
• It was noted for its advanced urban planning, architecture, and social organization.
 
 
 
• **Bronze Usage in Ancient Times**:
 
 
• Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin, known for its strength and durability.
 
• It was commonly used for making tools, weapons, and sculptures in ancient civilizations.

questions.question: Gold Monetisation Scheme (GMS) was launched by the Government of India in _________ .Under this scheme, one can deposit their gold in any form in a GMS account to earn interest as the price of the gold metal goes up.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**2015**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Gold Monetisation Scheme (GMS) was launched by the Government of India in November 2015.
 
• Under this scheme, individuals and institutions can deposit their gold in any form and earn interest on it as the price of gold appreciates.
 
• The scheme aims to mobilize idle gold lying with households and institutions and put it to productive use.
 
• Deposits can be made for short-term (1-3 years), medium-term (5-7 years), and long-term (12-15 years).
 
• Interest earned on gold deposits is exempt from capital gains tax, wealth tax, and income tax.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Eligibility:** The scheme is available to individuals, HUFs (Hindu Undivided Families), trusts, and companies.
 
• **Process:** Gold can be deposited in the form of bars, coins, or jewellery, which is then melted and assayed to determine purity and weight.
 
• **Redemption:** On maturity, the depositor can redeem the principal either in gold or its cash equivalent, along with the interest accrued.
 
• **Security:** The gold deposited under the scheme is kept secure in the vaults of banks and is fully insured.
 
• **Objectives:** The scheme aims to reduce India's reliance on gold imports, provide a fillip to the gems and jewellery sector, and bring down the current account deficit.
